title: PHY_102 — End of Semester Objective Exam

questions.q: A body carries a net charge of −4.8 × 10⁻⁷ C. How many excess electrons does it hold?
questions.why: Quantisation: n = |q|/e = 4.8 × 10⁻⁷ / 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹. The mantissa gives 4.8/1.6 = 3.0 and the powers give 10⁻⁷⁻⁽⁻¹⁹⁾ = 10¹², so n = 3.0 × 10¹² — a pure count, no units. This is her worked example. 3.0 × 10⁻²⁶ subtracts the exponents the wrong way round; 7.7 × 10⁻²⁶ multiplies the charge by e instead of dividing; 4.8 × 10¹² keeps the mantissa 4.8 without dividing by 1.6.

questions.q: A negatively charged rod is touched briefly to a neutral insulated metal sphere and then taken away. The sphere is left
options: positively charged, the opposite sign to the rod.
neutral overall, with the negative charge gathered on the near side.
negatively charged, the same sign as the rod.
neutral, because charge cannot cross a single point of contact.
questions.why: Touching is charging by conduction: charge flows across and is shared, so both bodies end with the SAME sign — negative. Opposite sign is the outcome of induction with grounding, not conduction; charge gathered on one side with no net charge is polarisation, which needs the rod held near and NOT touching; and charge does cross at contact, which is exactly what conduction means.

questions.q: A negatively charged rod is held near an insulated metal sphere, and the sphere is then earthed. To leave the sphere permanently charged you must
options: withdraw the rod first, then disconnect the earth wire.
withdraw the rod and disconnect the earth wire at the same instant.
earth the sphere only after the rod has been withdrawn.
disconnect the earth wire while the rod is still near, then withdraw the rod.
questions.why: With the rod still near, the repelled electrons have already escaped to earth. Breaking the earth connection first traps that deficit, and only then may the rod be withdrawn, leaving a net positive sphere. Withdrawing the rod first lets the electrons flow straight back up the earth wire and the sphere ends neutral; doing both at once is the same failure with better timing; and earthing after the rod has gone does nothing at all, because there is no longer a field to displace the free electrons.

questions.q: A body that acquires a positive charge by friction has
options: gained protons from the other body.
lost some of its protons to the other body.
lost some of its electrons to the other body.
had some of its neutrons converted into protons.
questions.why: Only electrons move in solids; protons are locked in nuclei. Positive means a deficit of electrons. Gaining or losing protons never happens in friction, and converting neutrons into protons invents a nuclear reaction to explain a rubbing. Both bodies end equal and opposite, because charge is transferred, never created.

questions.q: Identical metal spheres carrying +12 nC and −4 nC are brought into contact and then separated. Each sphere now carries
options: +4.0 nC on one and −4.0 nC on the other.
+12 nC and −4 nC, unchanged.
questions.why: Charge is conserved, so the total is (+12) + (−4) = +8 nC; the spheres are identical, so they share it equally: q' = (q₁ + q₂)/2 = +4.0 nC each. +8.0 nC is the correct total but not halved; +4.0 and −4.0 halves the two charges separately instead of sharing the total; and 'unchanged' ignores that contact between conductors shares charge.

questions.q: A charged rod attracts a small piece of neutral aluminium foil. This happens because the foil
options: has acquired a net charge of the opposite sign to the rod.
has acquired a net charge of the same sign as the rod.
has lost protons to the surrounding air.
is polarised, its near side acquiring the opposite charge, while its net charge stays zero.
questions.why: Bringing a charged rod near a conductor rearranges the free electrons: the near face takes the opposite sign and the far face the same sign, and because the near face is closer, attraction wins. The net charge is still exactly zero — this is polarisation, not charging, which is why the foil is attracted whichever sign the rod carries. Acquiring a net opposite charge would require earthing; acquiring the same sign would require contact and would give repulsion; and protons never leave a solid.

questions.q: Rubbing glass with silk transfers 2.5 × 10¹⁰ electrons from the glass to the silk. The resulting charges are
options: glass −4.0 nC, silk +4.0 nC.
glass +4.0 nC, silk +4.0 nC.
glass +4.0 nC, silk −4.0 nC.
glass +4.0 nC, silk neutral.
questions.why: q = ne = (2.5 × 10¹⁰)(1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹) = 4.0 × 10⁻⁹ C. The glass LOST electrons, so it is positive; the silk gained them, so it is negative, and (+4.0) + (−4.0) = 0 as conservation demands. Reversing the signs gets the direction of electron flow backwards; two positives and a positive-plus-neutral pair both create net charge out of nothing.

questions.q: Induction becomes more effective as the charged rod is brought closer to the conductor because
options: electrons begin to jump across the gap from the rod.
the conductor's own charge increases as the rod approaches.
the conductor's protons are pulled towards the near face.
the rod's field at the conductor is stronger, so more free electrons are displaced.
questions.why: Induction works by the rod's field pushing the conductor's free electrons; a stronger field at the conductor displaces more of them, and the field grows as the separation shrinks. Nothing crosses the gap — the moment charge jumps across it is conduction, not induction. Until the conductor is earthed its net charge stays zero, and protons never move.

questions.q: She writes Coulomb's law as F = k|q₁q₂|/r². The absolute-value bars are there because
options: charge is always a positive quantity.
the law as she states it gives a magnitude only; the direction comes from the diagram.
the force is always repulsive.
the bars indicate that the two charges must be equal in size.
questions.why: Her wording is 'the MAGNITUDE of the electric force … is directly proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance'. Magnitudes go into the formula, the answer comes out positive, and repulsion or attraction is read off the sketch — she never substitutes a signed charge. Charge is not always positive; the force is attractive for unlike signs; and the bars say nothing about the charges being equal.

questions.q: Which value of the electrostatic constant does she use throughout her deck, and in what role?
options: k = 9.0 × 10⁹ N m²/C², the multiplier in F = k|q₁q₂|/r².
ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C²/N m², the multiplier in F = ε₀|q₁q₂|/r².
μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m/A, the multiplier in F = μ₀|q₁q₂|/r².
k = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ N m²/C², the multiplier in F = k|q₁q₂|/r².
questions.why: Every number on her slides follows from k = 1/4πε₀ = 9.0 × 10⁹ N m²/C². Match it and your arithmetic matches hers; use a more precise value and you will get 574 N/C where her slide reads 575 and think you have erred. ε₀ appears only inside the definition of k and is never used numerically; μ₀ belongs to magnetism, weeks 8 to 12; and 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C is the elementary charge, not a constant of the force law.

questions.q: Two protons are 3.6 nm apart. She computes the two forces on an electron 1.2 nm from one of them as |F₁₃| = 16 × 10⁻¹¹ N and |F₂₃| = 4 × 10⁻¹¹ N. The total force on the electron is
options: 20 × 10⁻¹¹ N, toward the nearer proton.
16 × 10⁻¹¹ N, toward the nearer proton.
12 × 10⁻¹¹ N, toward the nearer proton.
12 × 10⁻¹¹ N, toward the farther proton.
questions.why: The electron is negative, so it is attracted to BOTH protons — and because they sit on opposite sides, the two attractions oppose. The vector sum is the difference, 16 − 4 = 12 × 10⁻¹¹ N, pointing toward the stronger pull, which is the nearer proton. (Her deck stops after the two magnitudes and never states this.) 20 × 10⁻¹¹ N adds two arrows that point opposite ways; 16 × 10⁻¹¹ N forgets the second proton entirely; and the direction toward the farther proton contradicts the fact that the nearer force is four times larger.

questions.q: In that same example she labels the distances r₁ = 1.2 nm = r and r₂ = 2.4 nm = 2r. The point of the labelling is that
options: doubling the separation halves the force, so |F₂₃| = |F₁₃|/2.
the force depends only on the ratio of the distances, not on their size.
doubling the separation quarters the force, so |F₂₃| = |F₁₃|/4.
the two forces must be equal because the two protons are identical.
questions.why: Coulomb's law is an inverse SQUARE law: the second denominator is (2r)² = 4r², so the second force is exactly a quarter of the first — 16 × 10⁻¹¹ becomes 4 × 10⁻¹¹, and you can write it down without recomputing. Halving is the inverse-first-power answer; the absolute distance matters as much as the ratio; and identical sources at different distances do not give equal forces.

questions.q: Her Example 2 has Q₁ = −18 μC at x = −9 m, Q₂ = −12 μC at x = +1 m and Q₃ = +24 μC at x = +7 m. She finds F₂₁ = 0.0194 N and F₃₁ = 0.0152 N. The net force on Q₁ is
options: 4.2 × 10⁻³ N in the −x direction.
3.46 × 10⁻² N in the −x direction.
4.2 × 10⁻³ N in the +x direction.
1.94 × 10⁻² N in the −x direction.
questions.why: Q₂ is negative and lies to the right, so it repels Q₁ leftward; Q₃ is positive and lies to the right, so it attracts Q₁ rightward. Taking +x as positive, her sum is ΣF = F₃₁ − F₂₁ = 0.0152 − 0.0194 = −0.0042 N, and the minus is a DIRECTION: 4.2 × 10⁻³ N along −x. Adding the two magnitudes gives 3.46 × 10⁻² N and ignores the free-body diagram; +x reverses the answer, since the nearer 12 μC beats the farther 24 μC once distance is squared; and 1.94 × 10⁻² N uses only one of the two forces.

questions.q: For the same three charges, the net electric force on Q₂ is
options: 5.26 × 10⁻² N in the +x direction.
9.14 × 10⁻² N in the −x direction.
1.94 × 10⁻² N in the +x direction.
9.14 × 10⁻² N in the +x direction.
questions.why: Q₁ is negative and lies to the left, so it repels Q₂ to the right; Q₃ is positive and lies to the right, so it attracts Q₂ to the right. Both arrows point +x, so the two forces ADD: F₁₂ = 0.0194 N and F₃₂ = 2.592/36 = 0.0720 N give 0.0914 N along +x. (Her slide sets this part and never solves it.) 5.26 × 10⁻² N subtracts them, which the diagram forbids; the −x direction reverses both contributions; and 1.94 × 10⁻² N leaves out the pull from Q₃.

questions.q: A 2.40 μC charge experiences a 3.00 mN force in an electric field. The magnitude of the field there is
questions.why: This is the defining equation, not the point-charge formula: E = F/q₀ = (3.00 × 10⁻³)/(2.40 × 10⁻⁶) = 1.25 × 10³ N/C. No value of k appears anywhere; the whole problem is the prefix conversion m = 10⁻³ and μ = 10⁻⁶. 1250 N is the right number with the wrong unit — a field is newtons per coulomb, not newtons; 8.00 × 10⁻⁴ divides the charge by the force; and 7.20 × 10⁻⁹ multiplies them.

questions.q: What are the magnitude and direction of the electric field due to a −6.8 μC point charge at a distance of 7.4 m?
options: 1.1 × 10³ N/C, directed radially outward from the charge.
1.1 × 10³ N/C, directed radially inward toward the charge.
8.3 × 10³ N/C, directed radially inward toward the charge.
−1.1 × 10³ N/C, directed radially outward from the charge.
questions.why: |E| = k|Q|/r² = 9.0 × 10⁹ × 6.8 × 10⁻⁶ / 7.4² = 6.12 × 10⁴ / 54.76 = 1.1 × 10³ N/C, and the source is negative, so the field points radially INWARD. Note she declares Q = −6.8 × 10⁻⁶ C and then substitutes the magnitude, because |E| is a magnitude. Outward is the field of a positive charge; 8.3 × 10³ N/C divides by 7.4 instead of 7.4²; and a negative magnitude comes from feeding the signed charge into a formula whose left-hand side is |E|. (Her slide gives the number but omits the direction the question asks for.)

questions.q: A +2.00 nC charge sits at the origin and a −5.00 nC charge at x = 0.800 m. The electric field at x = 0.200 m is
options: 450 N/C in the +x direction.
325 N/C in the +x direction.
575 N/C in the +x direction.
520 N/C in the +x direction.
questions.why: E₁ points away from the positive charge, so rightward; E₂ points toward the negative charge, which lies further right, so rightward too — same direction, so the magnitudes add. E₁ = 9.0 × 10⁹ × 2 × 10⁻⁹/(0.200)² = 450 N/C and E₂ = 9.0 × 10⁹ × 5 × 10⁻⁹/(0.600)² = 125 N/C, giving 575 N/C along +x. 450 N/C is E₁ alone; 325 N/C subtracts the two although both arrows agree; and 520 N/C uses 0.800 m for the second distance instead of the source-to-field-point distance 0.600 m — the single commonest way to lose this problem.

questions.q: An electron is then placed at that point, where E = 575 N/C along +x. The force on it is
options: 9.2 × 10⁻¹⁷ N in the +x direction.
9.2 × 10⁻¹⁷ N in the −x direction.
5.75 × 10² N in the −x direction.
3.6 × 10²¹ N in the −x direction.
questions.why: F = |q|E = (1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹)(575) = 9.2 × 10⁻¹⁷ N, and because the electron's charge is negative the force is ANTIPARALLEL to E, so along −x. Nothing about the field changed; only the sign of q. The +x direction is the force on a positive charge; 5.75 × 10² N quotes the field's number as a force; and 3.6 × 10²¹ N divides by e instead of multiplying. (Her deck sets this and never answers it.)

questions.q: One of her slides is headed 'ELECTRIC FIELD AROUND A POSITIVE CHARGE, − Q' and its body reads 'the direction of the electric field is radially inward'. The correct reading is
options: the body text is wrong; the field around a positive charge is radially outward.
both are right, because the field around any charge is radially inward.
the magnitude formula must change sign for a negative charge.
the heading is a misprint for NEGATIVE charge; the field around −Q is radially inward.
questions.why: The body text and the diagram — arrows pointing in toward a minus sphere — are both correct; only the word POSITIVE in the heading is wrong. Do not copy it into a script. The body text is not the error; the field around a positive charge is outward, so 'always inward' is false; and the magnitude formula |E| = k|Q|/r² is identical for both signs — only the arrow changes.

questions.q: A cell of emf 1.5 V and internal resistance 0.5 Ω drives an external resistor of 2.5 Ω. The current is
questions.why: Round the whole loop, ε = I(R + r), so I = 1.5/(2.5 + 0.5) = 0.50 A. 0.60 A is ε/R, leaving the internal resistance out of the sum — the standard error, and it always gives too large a current; 0.75 A subtracts r instead of adding it; 2.0 A inverts the fraction, dividing (R + r) by ε, which would give ohms per volt.

questions.q: For that same cell and load, the terminal potential difference is
questions.why: V = ε − Ir = 1.5 − (0.50)(0.5) = 1.25 V, and the check V = IR = (0.50)(2.5) = 1.25 V agrees. 1.5 V is the emf, which equals the terminal p.d. only when no current flows; 1.75 V adds the lost volts instead of subtracting them, which is the charging case; and 0.25 V is the lost volts Ir themselves, dissipated inside the cell.

questions.q: A cell on varying load gives (I, V) readings of (0.20 A, 1.40 V) and (0.80 A, 1.10 V). Its emf and internal resistance are
questions.why: V = ε − rI is a straight line: the gradient is (1.10 − 1.40)/(0.80 − 0.20) = −0.50 V/A, so r = 0.50 Ω, and extrapolating to I = 0 gives ε = 1.40 + (0.20)(0.50) = 1.50 V. Taking 1.40 V as the intercept reads off a measured point rather than the extrapolation; 2.0 Ω is the negative RECIPROCAL of the slope, which has units of siemens, not ohms; and a negative resistance confuses the sign of the gradient with the value of r.

questions.q: A rod of length 0.50 m slides at 3.0 m/s across a field of 0.40 T perpendicular to the circuit, whose total resistance is 2.0 Ω. The emf and current are
options: 0.60 V and 1.2 A
6.0 V and 3.0 A
questions.why: Motional emf ε = Bvl = (0.40)(3.0)(0.50) = 0.60 V, and Ohm's law gives I = ε/R = 0.60/2.0 = 0.30 A. Check the energy: F = BIl = 0.060 N, mechanical power Fv = 0.18 W, electrical power I²R = 0.18 W. 1.2 A multiplies by R instead of dividing; 0.20 V leaves the speed out of Bvl; and 6.0 V is a power-of-ten slip carried straight through into the current.

questions.q: A defibrillator capacitor of 100 μF is charged to 5.0 kV. The energy stored is
questions.why: U = ½CV² = ½(100 × 10⁻⁶)(5.0 × 10³)² = ½(10⁻⁴)(2.5 × 10⁷) = 1250 J. Delivered in 2.0 ms that is 6.25 × 10⁵ W — huge power from a modest battery, because the fill is slow and the release fast. 2500 J is QV without the factor of a half, which is the work when the p.d. is held constant, not while it rises from zero; 0.25 J forgets to square the voltage; and 1.25 J loses three powers of ten in the microfarads.

questions.q: A parallel-plate capacitor in vacuum has A = 0.02 m² and d = 0.005 m. Its capacitance is
questions.why: C = ε₀A/d = (8.85 × 10⁻¹² × 0.02)/0.005 = 1.77 × 10⁻¹³/0.005 = 3.54 × 10⁻¹¹ F. The deck prints 3.54 × 10⁻¹² F for exactly this data — one power of ten low, and it is a misprint, not a rounding, so use 3.54 × 10⁻¹¹ F. 3.54 × 10⁻¹⁰ F is a power of ten the other way; 1.77 × 10⁻¹¹ F halves the answer, mixing in the ½ that belongs to the energy formula.

questions.q: For that capacitor with E = 200 N/C between the plates, the deck reports 1.77 × 10⁻⁷ J. That figure is really
options: the total stored energy in joules, and the deck is correct.
the energy density in J/m³; the total energy is 1.77 × 10⁻³ J.
the capacitance in farads, mislabelled.
the energy density in J/m³; the total energy is 1.77 × 10⁻¹¹ J.
questions.why: u_E = ½ε₀E² = ½(8.85 × 10⁻¹²)(200)² = 1.77 × 10⁻⁷, and that expression is an energy DENSITY, so the unit is J/m³. Multiply by the volume Ad = 0.02 × 0.005 = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ m³ to get the total, U = 1.77 × 10⁻¹¹ J — which the other route, ½CV² with C = 3.54 × 10⁻¹¹ F and V = Ed = 1.0 V, confirms. The deck's 'J' is wrong; 1.77 × 10⁻³ J multiplies by the volume the wrong way; and the number is not a capacitance.

questions.q: Which pair of statements correctly distinguishes a conductor from an insulator?
options: A conductor has free electrons and a high resistivity; an insulator has bound electrons and zero internal field.
A conductor has free electrons and zero internal field in electrostatic equilibrium; an insulator has bound electrons and a high resistivity.
A conductor has zero internal field because it has no electrons; an insulator has a field because it has many.
An insulator is a conductor that simply needs a larger voltage before it conducts normally.
questions.why: The three differences named in the course are exactly these: whether electrons are free to move, whether a field can exist inside the material, and whether it facilitates or resists the flow of electricity. A conductor's free charges rearrange until the internal field is exactly zero, and its resistivity is low. Swapping resistivity and internal field describes neither material; a conductor is full of electrons, not empty of them; and pushed far enough an insulator breaks down rather than conducting normally, so it is not just a conductor with a higher threshold.

questions.q: A slide says the internal resistance of a cell is 'the negative reciprocal of the slope' of the V–I graph. This is wrong because
options: the slope is positive, so no minus sign belongs there at all.
the internal resistance is read from the intercept, not the slope.
the graph of V against I is not a straight line.
the slope of V against I is already in volts per ampere, i.e. ohms, so r = −(slope).
questions.why: Check the units, which is the fastest test available: V/A is the ohm, so minus the slope IS the resistance and a reciprocal would give siemens. The slope really is negative, since V falls as I rises, so the minus sign is needed; the intercept gives the emf, not r; and for a source of constant emf and constant internal resistance the line is straight, which is why the method works.

questions.q: When a linear circuit is analysed by superposition, the sources that are not currently acting are replaced as follows:
options: an ideal voltage source by an open circuit, an ideal current source by a short circuit.
both by short circuits.
an ideal voltage source by a short circuit, an ideal current source by an open circuit.
both by open circuits.
questions.why: Ask what a dead element forces. A zeroed voltage source holds 0 V across itself at any current — that is a wire, a short. A zeroed current source passes 0 A at any voltage — that is a break, an open circuit. Swapping the two is the commonest superposition error; treating both alike destroys the distinction between the two source types altogether.

questions.q: In a network, two sources acting separately each drive 0.75 A through a 4.0 Ω branch in the same direction. With both sources present, the current and the power in that branch are
options: 1.50 A and 4.5 W
1.50 A and 9.0 W
questions.why: Currents and voltages superpose, so 0.75 + 0.75 = 1.50 A. Powers do NOT, because P = I²R is quadratic: the true power is (1.50)²(4.0) = 9.0 W. 4.5 W adds the two single-source powers, 2 × (0.75)²(4.0), which is the error the rule exists to forbid; 0.75 A ignores the second source; and 2.25 W is one source's power quoted alongside the combined current.

questions.q: A load is removed from a network and the voltage across the open terminals measured as 8.00 V; with the load in place the same node sat at 6.00 V. The Thévenin voltage of the network is
options: 6.00 V, the voltage measured with the load in place.
2.00 V, the difference between the two readings.
14.00 V, the sum of the two readings.
8.00 V, the open-circuit voltage.
questions.why: V_Th is defined as the OPEN-circuit voltage: delete the load first, then measure. Here that is 8.00 V, and reconnecting a 4.0 Ω load in series with R_Th = 1.333 Ω duly gives 8.00/5.333 = 1.50 A, matching the direct solution. The 6.00 V reading is the loaded node voltage, which is what V_Th plus R_Th is designed to predict, not what it equals; and neither the difference nor the sum of the two readings is a defined quantity.

questions.q: Charges of +2.0 nC and −2.0 nC are held 1.0 mm apart. The electric dipole moment of the pair is
options: 4.0 × 10⁻¹² C·m, directed from −q toward +q.
2.0 × 10⁻⁹ C·m, directed from +q toward −q.
2.0 × 10⁻¹² C·m, directed from −q toward +q.
zero, because the two charges cancel.
questions.why: p = qd uses the magnitude of ONE charge times the separation: (2.0 × 10⁻⁹)(1.0 × 10⁻³) = 2.0 × 10⁻¹² C·m, and in physics convention it points from the negative charge to the positive one. 4.0 × 10⁻¹² C·m adds the two charges, which is meaningless for an object that is neutral overall; 2.0 × 10⁻⁹ C·m leaves the separation in millimetres and also reverses the direction (that is the chemistry convention); and the moment is not zero — the net CHARGE cancels, which is precisely why the dipole moment is the quantity that survives.

questions.q: For a short dipole, the field on the axis and the field on the perpendicular bisector, at the same distance r, are related by
options: axial = 2 × equatorial, axial parallel to p and equatorial antiparallel to p.
axial = ½ × equatorial, axial parallel to p and equatorial antiparallel to p.
they are equal in magnitude and both parallel to p.
axial = 2 × equatorial, and both are parallel to p.
questions.why: Axial E = 2kp/r³ and equatorial E = kp/r³ — same 1/r³ law, factor of two apart. On the axis you are nearer one charge, so the field runs the way p does; on the bisector the components along p survive and point from +q toward −q, i.e. ANTIPARALLEL to p. Halving inverts the ratio; equal magnitudes ignore the factor of two; and making both parallel loses the sign reversal on the bisector.

questions.q: A dipole of moment 2.0 × 10⁻¹² C·m sits in a uniform field of 3.0 × 10⁵ N/C with p at 30° to the field. The torque on it and the net force on it are
options: 5.2 × 10⁻⁷ N·m and zero.
3.0 × 10⁻⁷ N·m and zero.
zero and zero.
questions.why: τ = pE sin θ = (2.0 × 10⁻¹²)(3.0 × 10⁵)(0.500) = 3.0 × 10⁻⁷ N·m, and in a UNIFORM field the forces qE and −qE on the two ends are equal and opposite, so the net force is exactly zero — the dipole turns but does not translate. 5.2 × 10⁻⁷ uses cos 30°, which belongs to the energy U = −pE cos θ, not the torque; a non-zero net force needs a non-uniform field; and the torque vanishes only at θ = 0° or 180°.

questions.q: A charged parallel-plate capacitor is disconnected from its battery and a dielectric of constant κ = 5.0 is then slid between the plates. Compared with before,
options: Q is unchanged, C is 5 times larger, and V and E are 5 times smaller.
V is unchanged, C is 5 times larger, and Q is 5 times larger.
Q is unchanged, C is 5 times smaller, and V is 5 times larger.
Q, C, V and E are all unchanged, because the dielectric is an insulator.
questions.why: The test is whether the source is still connected. Disconnected means the charge is trapped: Q is fixed, C = κC₀ rises by 5, so V = Q/C and E = V/d both fall by 5 — a 177 pF capacitor at 100 V becomes 885 pF at 20 V. Holding V fixed while Q rises fivefold is the constant-VOLTAGE case, which needs the battery left attached; capacitance never falls when a dielectric is inserted; and 'nothing changes' ignores the polarisation of the slab, which is exactly what reduces the internal field.

questions.q: Resistors of 4 Ω, 6 Ω and 10 Ω are connected in parallel. The equivalent resistance is
questions.why: 1/R_eq = 1/4 + 1/6 + 1/10 = 15/60 + 10/60 + 6/60 = 31/60, and then INVERT: R_eq = 60/31 = 1.94 Ω. Check it against the rule that a parallel equivalent is always below the smallest branch, and 1.94 < 4. 0.52 Ω is 31/60 left uninverted, the single commonest lost mark here; 20 Ω applies the series rule; and 6.67 Ω is the average of the three, which is not a rule at all.

questions.q: Resistors of 3 Ω, 5 Ω, 9 Ω and 10 Ω are connected in series. The equivalent resistance is
questions.why: R_eq = R₁ + R₂ + R₃ + R₄ = 3 + 5 + 9 + 10 = 27 Ω, and it must land ABOVE the largest single resistor, which 27 > 10 confirms. 1.30 Ω applies the parallel formula and inverts; 10 Ω quotes the largest resistor alone; and 0.77 Ω is the sum of reciprocals left uninverted. Series adds and goes up; parallel adds reciprocals and comes down.

questions.q: In her definitions, a junction is a point where
options: two or more conductors meet; a loop is any path between two points.
the current changes direction; a loop is any circuit containing a battery.
a resistor meets a battery; a loop is any mesh with no junction in it.
three or more conductors meet; a loop is any closed conducting path.
questions.why: Her slide is explicit — three or more conductors for a junction, and any closed conducting path for a loop — and her figure prints 'Not a Junction' on two corners where only two conductors meet. At a two-conductor point the current has nowhere to divide, so the junction rule has nothing to say. The other options loosen the definition until every corner counts as a junction, which is exactly the mistake the labelled figure is there to prevent.

questions.q: Kirchhoff's two rules rest on which conservation laws?
options: ΣI = 0 expresses conservation of energy; ΣV = 0 expresses conservation of charge.
ΣI = 0 at a junction expresses conservation of charge; ΣV = 0 round a loop expresses conservation of energy.
Both express conservation of charge.
Both express conservation of energy.
questions.why: Her Summary slide states it in those words: no charge can accumulate at a junction, so what enters per second leaves per second; and the potential changes round a closed loop must sum to zero, because a charge returned to its starting point has gained no energy. Swapping the two, or attaching both to one law, loses the reason each rule is true and the reason there are two of them rather than one.

questions.q: Travelling round a loop, you cross a battery from its − terminal to its + terminal, and you pass through a resistor in the same direction as the assumed current. The two terms enter the loop equation as
options: −ε and −IR
+ε and +IR
+ε and −IR
−ε and +IR
questions.why: Her four sign rules: crossing a source from − to + is +ε and from + to − is −ε; walking through a resistor WITH the assumed current is −IR, because the current runs downhill in potential, and against it is +IR, a rise. The emf sign depends only on the order in which you cross the terminals, never on which way the current runs, and the IR sign depends only on the travel direction relative to the current arrow. Each of the other combinations flips one of those two independent rules.

questions.q: Her Example 1 loop is −I(4 Ω) − 4 V − I(7 Ω) + 12 V − I(2 Ω) − I(3 Ω) = 0. The current is
questions.why: Collect the emfs, 12 − 4 = 8 V, and the resistances, 4 + 7 + 2 + 3 = 16 Ω, so 8 V = I(16 Ω) and I = 0.5 A. Since I comes out positive, the assumed direction was right. 1.0 A adds the two emfs as 16 V instead of subtracting the opposing 4 V; 0.8 A uses only the two external resistors, 3 + 7 = 10 Ω, and drops the batteries' internal 2 Ω and 4 Ω; 2.0 A inverts the final division.

questions.q: In that circuit, with I = 0.5 A, the potential difference V_ab found by the lower path is (0.5)(7) + 4 + (0.5)(4). Its value, and the check by the upper path, are
questions.why: The lower path gives 3.5 + 4 + 2 = 9.5 V, and walking b to a over the top gives +12 for the battery crossed − to +, then −1.0 and −1.5 for the two resistors crossed with the current: 9.5 V again. Two independent routes agreeing IS the loop rule, and it is the fastest way to catch a sign error. Adding the two upper IR terms instead of subtracting them walks those resistors against the current although the travel is with it, and the routes ending at 5.5 V or 1.5 V mix resistors from the wrong branches into the sum.

questions.q: In the same circuit the power output of each emf is P₁₂ᵥ = (12)(0.5) = 6 W and P₄ᵥ = (−4)(0.5) = −2 W. The negative value means
options: an arithmetic error has been made, since power cannot be negative.
the 4 V battery delivers 2 W in the opposite direction round the loop.
the assumed current direction must be reversed and the problem redone.
the 4 V battery is being charged, absorbing 2 W rather than delivering it.
questions.why: The stronger battery drives current INTO the 4 V battery's + terminal, so it is being charged and its power output is negative — it absorbs 2 W. The books balance: 6 − 2 = 4 W delivered, and I²R = (0.5)²(16) = 4 W dissipated. A negative power output is a legitimate answer, not an error; power is not a direction, so 'delivers in the opposite direction' is meaningless; and the current came out positive, so nothing needs reversing.

questions.q: Solving a network gives one branch current as −0.67 A. The correct response is
options: accept it: the magnitude is 0.67 A and the true direction is opposite to the assumed arrow.
redraw the arrow and solve the whole network again.
take the magnitude and keep the assumed direction.
treat it as an impossible result and check for an arithmetic error.
questions.why: Her remark after Example 1 is 'since I is positive, our assumed current direction is correct', and the corollary is that a negative current has the right size with the arrow reversed. Nothing is redone — the algebra has corrected your guess for you, which is why you are allowed to guess. Re-solving wastes exam time and gives the same number; keeping the assumed direction discards the information the minus sign carries; and a negative current is not an error at all.

questions.q: The rms value of an alternating current is defined as
options: the average of the current over one complete cycle.
the average of the current over one half-cycle.
the maximum instantaneous current reached during a cycle.
the steady direct current that would dissipate the same power in the same resistive load.
questions.why: Her slide defines it by equal heating: 'the equivalent direct current (DC) value that would produce the same amount of power dissipation in a resistive load'. That, not the shape of the curve, is what fixes it. The full-cycle average is zero, which is precisely why the rms was needed; the half-cycle mean is a different quantity (2/π of the peak) that she labels on a diagram and never uses; and the maximum instantaneous value is the PEAK.

questions.q: The peak value of a waveform is
options: the full swing from the trough to the crest.
the rms value multiplied by 2.
the maximum instantaneous value in a cycle, measured from the zero reference point.
the average of the positive half-cycle.
questions.why: Her wording: 'the highest point of the waveform … typically measured from the zero reference point'. The trough-to-crest swing is twice the peak and the deck never names or uses it; the rms-to-peak factor is √2 = 1.4142, not 2; and the half-cycle average is a different quantity again.

questions.q: A source has a frequency of 60.0 Hz. Its angular frequency is
options: 60.0 rad/s
9.55 rad/s
377 rad/s
questions.why: ω = 2πf = 2π(60.0) = 377 rad s⁻¹, and the ωt inside sin ωt is an angle in RADIANS. Writing sin(60t) uses f where ω belongs and is out by a factor of 6.28; 9.55 divides by 2π instead of multiplying; and 0.0167 s is the period T, not an angular frequency.

questions.q: Why does she square the current before averaging it?
options: Squaring converts the current into power directly, which is what a meter reads.
Squaring removes the frequency from the problem.
Because the average of I² equals the square of the average of I.
The full-cycle average of I is zero, but I² is never negative, and its average is ½I²_max.
questions.why: Her argument in three moves: the plain average carries no information because the positive and negative half-cycles cancel; squaring destroys the sign so the negative half stops cancelling the positive; and the squared wave oscillates between 0 and I²_max with its mean line at exactly half, giving (I²)_av = ½I²_max and hence I_rms = 0.7071 I_max. Read the name backwards — root of the mean of the square, in that order. Squaring gives I², not power, until you multiply by R; the frequency was never in the calculation; and the average of a square is emphatically not the square of the average, which is the whole point.

questions.q: A household circuit operates at an rms voltage of 120 V. The peak voltage is
questions.why: V_max = V_rms √2 = 120 × 1.4142 = 169.7, which she rounds to 170 V. Going rms to peak the answer must get BIGGER, because the rms value of a sinusoid is always less than its peak. 84.9 V multiplies by 0.7071 instead, the factor used the wrong way; 240 V doubles rather than multiplying by √2; and 120 V is the value you started with.

questions.q: Her practice question 2 is set with a house ac voltage of 120 V but solved with 250 V, and an ac current of 10 A. The defensible position in an exam is
options: the deck misprints the voltage; be able to give 170 V from 120 V and 353.56 V from 250 V, with 14.14 A either way.
only 353.56 V and 14.14 A, since the solution slide is the authoritative one.
only 170 V and 7.07 A, since the question slide is the authoritative one.
the question cannot be answered, because the two slides contradict each other.
questions.why: Slide 13 sets 120 V and slide 14 solves 250 V, and the deck never reconciles them; the likely reason for the change is that 120 V would repeat the answer to question 1. The method is identical whichever figure appears, so carry both: 120/0.7071 = 170 V and 250/0.7071 = 353.56 V. The current part is unaffected — 10/0.7071 = 14.14 A, so 7.07 A has the factor upside down — and refusing to answer throws away marks for a misprint that costs nothing to name.

questions.q: An AC generator of maximum voltage 24.0 V and frequency 60.0 Hz feeds a 265 Ω resistor. The rms voltage and rms current are
questions.why: V_rms = 0.7071 × 24 = 17.0 V, and then Ohm's law with rms on BOTH sides: I_rms = V_rms/R = 17/265 = 0.0642 A. 0.0906 A is V_max/R, which gives the peak current, not the rms one; the pair 24.0 V and 0.0906 A never converts to rms at all; and 0.0454 A applies the 0.7071 a second time to an already-converted figure, the standard way to halve your own answer.

questions.q: For that same circuit the average and maximum powers dissipated in the resistor are
questions.why: P_av = V²_rms/R = 17²/265 = 1.09 W and P_max = V²_max/R = 24²/265 = 2.174 W. The ratio is fixed at (V_max/V_rms)² = 2, so peak power in a resistor is exactly twice the average, always. Reversing the two makes the peak smaller than the mean; equal values would require the waveform to be flat; and the pair 0.0642 W and 24.0 W simply quotes the current and the peak voltage as powers.

questions.q: In that problem the given frequency of 60.0 Hz is
options: not needed, because none of V_rms, I_rms, P_av or P_max depends on frequency in a pure resistor.
needed, to convert the peak voltage to the rms voltage.
needed, to find the reactance of the circuit.
needed, because average power depends on how many cycles occur per second.
questions.why: The load is a pure resistor: current and voltage stay in step, the conversion factor 0.7071 has no frequency in it, and P = V²/R has none either. Recognising a redundant given is itself an exam skill. The rms conversion is a fixed number; reactance requires an inductor or capacitor, which this circuit does not have and which belongs to the following week; and the average power is an average per cycle, so the number of cycles cancels out.

questions.q: For a supply v = V₀ sin ωt driving a current i = I₀ sin(ωt − φ), the average power over a complete cycle is
options: V_rms I_rms
V_rms I_rms cos φ
V_rms I_rms sin φ
V₀ I₀ cos φ
questions.why: The instantaneous product splits into a constant term (V₀I₀/2) cos φ and a ripple at twice the supply frequency whose average over a cycle is zero. All of the average power therefore sits in the constant term: P = ½V₀I₀ cos φ = V_rms I_rms cos φ. V_rms I_rms alone is the APPARENT power S in volt-amperes, right only when the power factor is 1; V_rms I_rms sin φ is the REACTIVE power Q in var; and V₀I₀ cos φ uses peak values and is twice too large, because AC power formulae take rms values throughout.

questions.q: The Week 7 deck states that 'in a purely reactive AC circuit the power can be calculated using P = V × I × sin θ'. The correct position is
options: the expression is correct, and gives the power in watts.
the expression is correct but should use cos θ instead of sin θ.
the expression gives the apparent power in volt-amperes.
that expression is the reactive power Q in var; the average real power in a pure reactance is zero.
questions.why: VI sin φ is the rate at which energy is borrowed and returned, measured in volt-amperes reactive, not consumed. In a purely reactive circuit φ = ±90°, so the whole of the apparent power is reactive and the real power is exactly zero — which is what the same deck says two slides later when it states that reactances do not dissipate energy. Calling it watts contradicts that; replacing sin by cos would give zero in a pure reactance and so cannot be what the slide meant to say; and the apparent power is VI with no trigonometric factor at all.

questions.q: A 30 Ω resistor in series with a 127 mH inductor is connected to a 200 V rms, 50 Hz supply. The impedance and current are
questions.why: X_L = 2πfL = 2π(50)(0.127) = 40.0 Ω, and R and X combine in QUADRATURE: Z = √(30² + 40²) = √2500 = 50.0 Ω, so I = V/Z = 200/50.0 = 4.00 A. 70.0 Ω adds R and X_L arithmetically, which is the standard wrong answer; 40.0 Ω uses the reactance alone and forgets the resistor; and 6.67 A divides the supply by R alone.

questions.q: For that same RL circuit, the real power consumed is
questions.why: P = VI cos φ with cos φ = R/Z = 30/50 = 0.600 lagging, so P = (200)(4.00)(0.600) = 480 W, confirmed by I²R = (16.0)(30) = 480 W. 800 W is the apparent power VI in volt-amperes, not watts; 1333 W is V²/R with the SUPPLY voltage, which is legal only when the whole supply sits across R — here only 120 V does, and 120²/30 = 480 W; 640 W is the reactive power VI sin φ in var.

questions.q: A series circuit has R = 12 Ω, X_L = 5 Ω and X_C = 21 Ω. Its impedance is
options: 28.6 Ω, and the current leads the voltage.
20.0 Ω, and the current leads the voltage.
20.0 Ω, and the current lags the voltage.
38.0 Ω, and the current lags the voltage.
questions.why: The reactances are 180° apart, so they SUBTRACT before anything is squared: X = X_L − X_C = 5 − 21 = −16 Ω. Then Z = √(12² + 16²) = √400 = 20.0 Ω, and because the net reactance is capacitive the current LEADS. 28.6 Ω comes from √(144 + 676), adding the two reactances instead of subtracting them; lagging is the inductive case, which requires X_L to win; and 38.0 Ω adds all three quantities arithmetically.

questions.q: A load draws 480 W of real power and 640 var of reactive power. Its apparent power is
options: 800 VA
160 VA
questions.why: The three powers form a right-angled triangle, S² = P² + Q²: √(480² + 640²) = √640000 = 800 VA. They never add arithmetically, so 1120 VA is wrong; 160 VA subtracts them; and the unit matters — apparent power is measured in volt-amperes, because only the real component is watts and only the watts are billed.

questions.q: A workshop draws 4.4 kW at 220 V rms with a power factor of 0.80 lagging. Its line current, and the line current after correction to unity power factor, are
options: 20.0 A, falling to 16.0 A.
25.0 A, falling to 31.3 A.
20.0 A, rising to 25.0 A.
25.0 A, falling to 20.0 A.
questions.why: S = P/PF = 4400/0.80 = 5500 VA, so I = S/V = 5500/220 = 25.0 A. Correction leaves the real power untouched, so afterwards I = P/V = 4400/220 = 20.0 A — the same 4.4 kW delivered by 20 A instead of 25, cutting the cable's I²R loss by 36 %. 20.0 A as the starting current forgets to divide by the power factor; the current cannot rise, since that would mean more volt-amperes for the same watts; and a rise from 20.0 A to 25.0 A runs the correction backwards.

questions.q: A series circuit of R = 10 Ω, L = 0.20 H and C = 20 μF is driven at its resonant frequency by a 100 V rms supply. At resonance
options: Z = 0 and the power factor is undefined.
Z is a maximum and the current is a minimum.
Z = 10 Ω, the power factor is 1 and P = 1000 W.
the power factor is 1 but no power is consumed, because L and C cancel.
questions.why: At ω₀ = 1/√(LC) = 500 rad/s (f₀ = 79.6 Hz), X_L = X_C = 100 Ω and they cancel, leaving Z = R = 10 Ω, φ = 0 and PF = 1. The current is then a maximum, 10.0 A, and P = V²/R = 1000 W. Z falls to R, not to zero — the resistance is still there; a series circuit at resonance has minimum impedance and maximum current, not the reverse; and the power is maximum, not zero: what cancels is the reactance, not the dissipation.

questions.q: A bar magnet is cut in half across its middle. The result is
options: one isolated north pole and one isolated south pole.
two shorter magnets, each with a full north and a full south pole.
two pieces that are no longer magnetic.
two magnets, each with two north poles.
questions.why: There are no magnetic monopoles: every line of B is a closed loop, so cutting a magnet simply makes two dipoles, and this continues down to the single atom, where the moment is a circulating or spinning charge. This is the one structural difference from electrostatics, where pulling a dipole apart really does leave two isolated charges. The remaining options would all require a lone pole to exist.

questions.q: A flat coil of 50 turns measuring 8.0 cm by 5.0 cm carries 2.0 A. Its magnetic dipole moment is
questions.why: μ = NIA with the area in SI: A = (0.080)(0.050) = 4.0 × 10⁻³ m², so μ = (50)(2.0)(4.0 × 10⁻³) = 0.40 A·m², directed along the normal by the right-hand rule. 4.0 × 10³ leaves the area in cm², which is wrong by 10⁴; 8.0 × 10⁻³ drops the factor N, the commonest omission; and A·m is not the unit — A·m², equivalently J/T, is.

questions.q: A current loop sits in a uniform field with the plane of the loop containing B. The torque on it is
options: zero, because the angle between the plane and B is 0°.
maximum, μB, because the angle between the normal and B is 90°.
maximum, μB, because the angle between the normal and B is 0°.
zero, because the net force on the loop is zero.
questions.why: In τ = μB sin θ, θ is the angle between the MOMENT (the normal to the loop) and B, never between the loop's plane and B. A plane containing B means a normal perpendicular to B, θ = 90°, sin θ = 1, and the torque is at its maximum. Reading the angle off the plane gives the answer exactly backwards; θ = 0 is the aligned position, where the torque vanishes; and the net force being zero says nothing about the couple — that is precisely the point of a uniform field.

questions.q: For a dipole of moment 0.40 A·m² in a field of 0.40 T, the work needed to turn it from aligned to anti-aligned is
options: zero
questions.why: U = −μB cos θ, so U(0°) = −μB = −0.16 J and U(180°) = +μB = +0.16 J, and the work is the difference, ΔU = 2μB = 0.32 J. 0.16 J is μB, the value of one end point rather than the gap between them; zero would follow if the torque were zero throughout, but the torque only vanishes AT the two ends; and 0.64 J doubles the answer again.

questions.q: A dipole placed in a uniform magnetic field experiences
options: a net force but no torque, so it translates without turning.
both a torque and a net force.
a torque but no net force, so it turns without translating.
neither, because the field is uniform.
questions.why: The forces on opposite sides of the loop are equal and opposite, so they sum to zero while still forming a couple. That is why a compass needle swings but does not fly across the room, and why a magnet attracted to a nail is a NON-uniform-field phenomenon: a net force needs a field gradient. A torque with no force is the uniform-field case; no torque at all would require the moment to be already aligned.

questions.q: A long straight wire carries 8.0 A. The magnetic flux density 4.0 cm from it is
options: 4.0 × 10⁻⁵ T, directed radially away from the wire.
4.0 × 10⁻⁵ T, tangential to a circle round the wire.
1.6 × 10⁻³ T, tangential to a circle round the wire.
4.0 × 10⁻⁵ T, directed along the wire.
questions.why: B = μ₀I/2πr = (2 × 10⁻⁷)(8.0)/(0.040) = 4.0 × 10⁻⁵ T, and the field lines are closed CIRCLES in planes perpendicular to the wire, with the sense given by the right-hand grip rule. Radially outward is the pattern of a line of charge, whose field also falls as 1/r but points somewhere completely different; 1.6 × 10⁻³ T leaves the distance in centimetres; and B is never along the current that produces it.

questions.q: A solenoid of 500 turns wound over 25 cm carries 3.0 A. The flux density inside it is
options: 7.5 × 10⁻³ T only if the radius is also known.
questions.why: B = μ₀nI with n = N/L = 500/0.25 = 2000 turns per metre: B = (4π × 10⁻⁷)(2000)(3.0) = 7.5 × 10⁻³ T, uniform and axial inside, essentially zero outside. 1.9 T uses N = 500 in place of n and is wrong by the factor L; 3.0 × 10⁻⁶ T loses the turns entirely; and the radius does not enter — B inside a long solenoid depends only on the core, the turns per metre and the current.

questions.q: The electron's magnetic moment is written M = g(−eL/2m). The minus sign means
options: the moment has a negative magnitude.
the moment is antiparallel to the angular momentum, because the electron's charge is negative.
the moment lowers the electron's energy in any field.
the g-factor itself is negative.
questions.why: The sign is a statement about DIRECTION: the conventional current circulates opposite to the electron's motion, so μ points against L. It is a different minus sign from the one in U = −μ·B, which is what makes alignment the low-energy state, and the two are unrelated. Magnitudes are never negative; the energy depends on the orientation, not on this sign; and g is a positive dimensionless number, about 1 for orbital motion and about 2 for spin (the deck calls it the 'correlation factor'; it is the g-factor).

questions.q: A charge of 2.5 C moves at 1.5 m/s where E = 5 N/C and B = 7.25 T. The deck answers 12.5 + 27.19 = 39.68 N. That answer is valid only if
options: the charge is positive, which is all that is required.
E and B are parallel to each other.
the speed is small enough for the magnetic term to be neglected.
v is perpendicular to B and the electric and magnetic forces happen to point the same way.
questions.why: F = q(E + v × B) is a VECTOR sum. Adding the two magnitudes needs both that sin θ = 1, so that the magnetic part really is 27.19 N, and that the two forces are parallel. Neither is given in the question. If E is parallel to B, the two forces are perpendicular and F = √(12.5² + 27.19²) = 29.9 N; if v is parallel to B the magnetic force vanishes and only the 12.5 N remains. The sign of the charge does not make two vectors collinear; parallel E and B is the case that breaks the arithmetic rather than justifying it; and the magnetic term here is the larger of the two.

questions.q: The magnetic force on a charge moving through a field is F = qvB sin θ. It is zero when
options: the velocity is perpendicular to B.
the velocity is parallel to B, or the charge is at rest.
the charge is negative.
the field is uniform.
questions.why: θ is the angle between v and B, so sin θ = 0 whenever the motion is along the field line, and a charge at rest has no magnetic force at all. This is why charged particles spiral ALONG field lines rather than crossing them. Perpendicular motion gives the MAXIMUM force, qvB; a negative charge feels the same size of force in the opposite direction; and uniformity has nothing to do with it — the electric term qE, by contrast, acts on a charge whether it moves or not.

questions.q: A slide states that 'work is done on moving charges when in a magnetic field'. The correct statement is
options: the magnetic force does work equal to qvB times the distance travelled.
the magnetic force is perpendicular to v, so it does no work and cannot change the particle's speed.
the magnetic force does work only when the charge moves parallel to the field.
the magnetic force does no work because it is always zero.
questions.why: Since F is perpendicular to v at every instant, the power F·v is exactly zero: the magnetic force changes the DIRECTION of the velocity and never its magnitude, so kinetic energy is constant after one lap or a million. Only the electric term does work. Work equal to qvB times the distance travelled ignores the perpendicularity; motion parallel to B gives zero force, not work; and the force is certainly not always zero — it is what bends the path.

questions.q: A proton (m = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, q = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) enters a 0.25 T field at 3.0 × 10⁶ m/s perpendicular to it. The radius of its path, and what happens to the period if the speed is doubled, are
options: 0.125 m; the period doubles.
0.125 m; the period is unchanged.
0.250 m; the period is unchanged.
0.0625 m; the period halves.
questions.why: Setting the magnetic force equal to the centripetal force, qvB = mv²/r gives r = mv/qB = (1.67 × 10⁻²⁷)(3.0 × 10⁶)/(4.00 × 10⁻²⁰) = 0.125 m. The period T = 2πm/qB contains no v at all: speed the proton up and the radius grows in exact proportion, so the lap time is identical — which is the whole basis of the cyclotron. The options that scale the period with speed have cancelled the velocity incorrectly, and 0.250 m and 0.0625 m mis-scale the radius.

questions.q: In a velocity selector, a charge passes straight through undeflected when
options: v = E/B, a condition that contains neither the charge nor the mass.
v = B/E, so that heavier particles are selected.
v = qE/B, so that the selected speed depends on the charge.
v = E/B, but only for positively charged particles.
questions.why: Balancing qE against qvB cancels q completely, leaving v = E/B — the same selected speed for electrons and for heavy positive ions, because both forces reverse together when the sign of the charge flips. That is what makes it a SPEED filter rather than a mass filter; mass only enters in a second, magnet-only stage, where r = mv/qB turns the device into a mass spectrometer. B/E has the ratio upside down, qE/B keeps a charge that must cancel, and the condition is not restricted to one sign.

questions.q: A straight wire of length 25 cm carries 8.0 A at 40° to a uniform field of 0.30 T. The force on it is
questions.why: F = BIL sin θ = (0.30)(8.0)(0.25)(sin 40°) = (0.60)(0.643) = 0.386 N, with θ measured between the CURRENT and B, and the force perpendicular to the plane containing them. 0.60 N is the maximum, which applies only when the wire is perpendicular to the field; 0.46 N uses cos 40°, inverting the two limiting cases — a wire laid along the field feels nothing, however large the current; and 39 N leaves the length in centimetres.

questions.q: The deck writes the force on a current element as dF = (I/c) dl × B. In the SI units used in every Miva calculation,
options: the factor should be 1/c², not 1/c.
the factor is correct and must be included.
the factor applies only when the wire is moving.
there is no factor of 1/c: dF = I dl × B.
questions.why: The 1/c belongs to the Gaussian (cgs) system. In SI the laws are F = qv × B and dF = I dl × B with no c anywhere, so dividing an answer by 3 × 10⁸ is a guaranteed loss of marks. A factor of 1/c² is not a form of the law in any system; retaining the c gives an answer 300 million times too small; and the motion of the wire is irrelevant to the units it is written in.

questions.q: Which statement about an electromagnetic wave in vacuum is correct?
options: E lies along the direction of propagation while B is perpendicular to it.
E and B are parallel to each other and perpendicular to the direction of travel.
E and B are perpendicular to each other and both perpendicular to the direction of travel, and c = fλ.
Longer wavelengths travel faster, which is why radio outruns light.
questions.why: The wave is transverse: an oscillating E generates an oscillating B and vice versa, with the two at right angles to each other and to the propagation direction, which is the direction of E × B. All frequencies travel at the same c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s in vacuum, so f and λ are inversely related — a 100 MHz FM signal has λ = 3.00 m, and gamma rays have the highest frequency and the shortest wavelength. A longitudinal E component is the standard wrong answer; parallel E and B is not a solution of the wave equations; and speed in vacuum does not depend on wavelength.

questions.q: A flat coil lies with its plane perpendicular to a uniform field B. The flux through it is
options: zero, because the plane is perpendicular to B.
BA, the maximum, because the normal is parallel to B.
BA sin θ, which cannot be evaluated without θ.
BA/2, the average of the maximum and zero.
questions.why: Φ = BA cos θ with θ measured from the NORMAL to the surface, never from the plane. A plane perpendicular to B means a normal parallel to B, θ = 0, cos θ = 1 and the flux is at its maximum. The sentence 'plane perpendicular to B' is the one students most often convert into θ = 90°, which is the edge-on orientation where the flux is zero. There is no unknown angle here, and there is no averaging rule.

questions.q: The emf induced in a coil depends on
options: the rate of change of the flux linkage, N dΦ/dt.
the flux linking the coil, NΦ.
the strength of the field, B, alone.
the number of turns and the area, but not on time.
questions.why: Faraday's law is ε = −N dΦ/dt: a coil sitting in the strongest steady field in the world has exactly zero emf, and a coil in a weak but rapidly changing field can have a large one. This is the single most common error in the whole topic. The flux itself, the field itself, and the coil's geometry all enter only through the RATE at which the flux linkage changes.

questions.q: A slide states that 'for Faraday's law to hold true there must be movement between the coil and the magnetic field'. The correct criterion is
options: relative motion, exactly as the slide says.
a changing current in the coil itself.
a changing flux, of which relative motion is only one cause — B, A or θ may change.
a change in the coil's resistance.
questions.why: Φ = BA cos θ can change in three independent ways: the field can change, the enclosed area can change, or the orientation can change. The deck contradicts its own sentence two slides later with the transformer, in which nothing moves at all and the emf comes entirely from a changing B. A changing current in the SAME coil is self-inductance, a special case rather than the criterion; and resistance affects the resulting current, never the emf.

questions.q: A 120-turn coil of radius 4.0 cm lies with its plane perpendicular to a field that falls steadily from 0.60 T to 0.10 T in 0.20 s. The induced emf is
questions.why: A = πr² = π(0.040)² = 5.03 × 10⁻³ m², ΔΦ = (0.50)(5.03 × 10⁻³) = 2.51 × 10⁻³ Wb, and ε = N ΔΦ/Δt = (120)(2.51 × 10⁻³)/0.20 = 1.5 V. All the physics is in the CHANGE, 0.50 T. 0.30 V substitutes the final field 0.10 T; 2.1 V uses the sum 0.70 T; and 150 V leaves the radius in centimetres, which multiplies the area by 10⁴.

questions.q: In that experiment the circuit resistance is 8.0 Ω and 38 mC circulates. If the same field change is made over 2.0 s instead of 0.20 s, the charge that circulates is
options: 3.8 mC, ten times smaller.
38 mC, unchanged.
380 mC, ten times larger.
zero, because the change is now too slow.
questions.why: q = N ΔΦ/R depends only on the TOTAL flux change and the resistance, not on how fast the change happens: slowing it down by ten divides the emf and the current by ten and multiplies the duration by ten, and the product is identical. This is the principle of the ballistic galvanometer and a favourite examiner's trap. The two scaled answers apply the time to the charge instead of to the current; and a slow change still induces an emf, merely a smaller one.

questions.q: A rod of length 0.25 m slides at 4.0 m/s on rails in a 0.35 T field, total circuit resistance 0.50 Ω. The retarding force on the rod is
options: 0.061 N, opposing the motion.
0.061 N, in the direction of motion.
0.35 N, opposing the motion.
zero, because the field is uniform.
questions.why: ε = BLv = 0.35 V, I = ε/R = 0.70 A and F = BIL = (0.35)(0.70)(0.25) = 0.061 N, equivalently B²L²v/R, and by Lenz's law it always opposes the motion. The power audit closes: Fv = 0.245 W and I²R = 0.245 W. A forward force would let the rod accelerate for ever while generating power, which is the perpetual-motion machine Lenz's law exists to forbid; 0.35 N quotes the emf as a force; and the force is not zero — a uniform field is exactly the condition assumed here.

questions.q: A coil of 200 turns and area 150 cm² rotates at 50 revolutions per second in a field of 0.080 T. Its peak emf is
questions.why: Convert first: A = 150 cm² = 1.50 × 10⁻² m², and ω = 2πf = 2π(50) = 314 rad/s. Then ε₀ = NBAω = (200)(0.080)(1.50 × 10⁻²)(314) = 75 V. 12 V uses f = 50 in place of ω and is short by the factor 2π, the commonest generator error; 0.075 V also leaves the area in cm²; and 53 V is the RMS value, ε₀/√2, which is what a meter would read but not what was asked.

questions.q: A solenoid has its number of turns doubled at the same length, area and current. Its self-inductance
options: doubles, because L is proportional to N.
quadruples, because L = μ₀N²A/ℓ.
is unchanged, because L depends only on the geometry.
halves, because the current is unchanged.
questions.why: Doubling the turns doubles the field (through n = N/ℓ) AND doubles the number of turns that the flux links, so L rises by a factor of four — N², not N, is the standard slip here. L does depend on geometry and core material only, never on the current in it, but the number of turns is part of that geometry, so 'unchanged' is wrong; and nothing here halves.

questions.q: Two coils have a mutual inductance M. Driving the 800-turn coil at 250 A/s induces 63 mV in the 150-turn coil. Driving the 150-turn coil at 250 A/s induces
options: 63 mV in the 800-turn coil, because M₁₂ = M₂₁.
336 mV in the 800-turn coil, in the ratio of the turns.
12 mV in the 800-turn coil, in the inverse ratio of the turns.
nothing, because mutual induction only works from the larger coil to the smaller.
questions.why: The reciprocity theorem says the mutual inductance is one number for the PAIR: it does not matter which coil you call the primary, so the same 0.251 mH at the same 250 A/s gives the same 63 mV. It is not obvious and it is examinable. The two scaled answers apply a turns ratio that reciprocity forbids, and induction is perfectly symmetric — a small coil driving a large one induces exactly as much as the reverse.

questions.q: The deck's own conclusion is that 'the actual existence of the magnetic flux is not sufficient to produce the induced emf; the flux must be changing'. Consequently a bar magnet held motionless deep inside a coil gives
options: no emf and no current, however strong the magnet.
a large steady emf, because the flux through the coil is large.
a small steady emf, proportional to the flux.
an alternating emf at the natural frequency of the coil.
questions.why: The emf is the RATE of change of flux, so a stationary magnet — large flux, zero rate — induces nothing at all. This is the same statement as ε = −N dΦ/dt with dΦ/dt = 0. A large steady emf and a small steady emf both confuse Φ with dΦ/dt, the defining error of the topic; and a coil has no natural frequency that could generate an alternating emf on its own.

questions.q: A loop lies in a uniform field directed out of the page, and the field is increasing. The induced current is
options: clockwise, so that its own field inside the loop points into the page.
anticlockwise, so that its own field inside the loop points out of the page.
clockwise, so that its own field inside the loop points out of the page.
zero, because the loop is not moving.
questions.why: Lenz's law opposes the CHANGE: the outward flux is growing, so the induced field inside the loop must point into the page to fight the increase, and by the right-hand grip rule that means a clockwise current. Anticlockwise would reinforce the increase and generate energy from nothing. Pairing a clockwise current with an out-of-the-page induced field contradicts the grip rule; and motion is not required — a changing field alone is enough.

questions.q: If instead the same outward field were DECREASING, the induced current would be
options: clockwise, its own field pointing into the page, since the induced field always opposes B.
anticlockwise, its own field pointing into the page.
anticlockwise, its own field pointing out of the page to replace the flux being lost.
zero, since a decreasing field cannot drive a current.
questions.why: The induced field opposes the CHANGE, not the field: falling flux is opposed by a current whose field points the SAME way as B, trying to maintain it, which the grip rule turns into an anticlockwise current. 'The induced field is always opposite to B' is wrong half the time, and this is the half. Pairing an anticlockwise current with an into-the-page induced field contradicts the grip rule; and a decreasing field is a changing field, so it certainly drives a current.

questions.q: A 200-turn coil of radius 5.0 cm lies with its plane perpendicular to a field that rises uniformly from 0.100 T to 0.500 T in 0.200 s. The induced emf is
questions.why: A = πr² = π(0.050)² = 7.854 × 10⁻³ m², dB/dt = 0.400/0.200 = 2.00 T/s, and ε = N A (dB/dt) = (200)(7.854 × 10⁻³)(2.00) = 3.14 V. 12.6 V uses the diameter where the radius belongs, quadrupling the area; 3.93 V substitutes the final field 0.500 T in place of the change 0.400 T; and 1.57 V takes dB/dt as 1.00 T/s, dividing the 0.400 T change by 0.400 s instead of by 0.200 s.

questions.q: For that coil, with a total circuit resistance of 8.0 Ω, the current and the charge circulated are
questions.why: I = ε/R = 3.14/8.0 = 0.393 A, and q = N|ΔΦ|/R = 200 × (7.854 × 10⁻³ × 0.400)/8.0 = 0.0785 C, which the independent check q = IΔt = 0.393 × 0.200 confirms. Quoting the current's number as a charge ignores the 0.200 s altogether; 25.1 A and 5.03 C multiply by R instead of dividing; and 3.93 × 10⁻⁴ C leaves the 200 turns out of the flux linkage.

questions.q: A 100-turn coil of area 0.020 m² rotates at 50 Hz in a field of 0.25 T. Its peak and rms emfs are
questions.why: ω = 2πf = 314.16 rad/s — the trap is that ω is not 50 — so ε_peak = NBAω = (100)(0.25)(0.020)(314.16) = 157.1 V, and ε_rms = 157.1/√2 = 111.1 V. 25.0 V uses f instead of ω and is short by 2π; the pair 157.1 V and 222.2 V multiplies by √2 rather than dividing, which would make the rms value exceed the peak; and the pair 111.1 V and 157.1 V swaps the two.

questions.q: A flat loop is described as 'inclined at 30° to a uniform field B'. The flux through it is
options: BA cos 30°, because the loop is at 30° to the field.
BA sin 60°, because the angle is measured in the plane.
zero, because the loop is not perpendicular to the field.
BA cos 60°, because the normal is at 60° to the field.
questions.why: The wording describes the PLANE, and θ in Φ = BA cos θ is measured from the normal, which is therefore at 90° − 30° = 60°: Φ = BA cos 60° = 0.5BA. Read the wording, then draw the normal. Using 30° directly reads the angle off the plane; BA sin 60° happens to equal BA cos 30° and makes the same error; and the flux is only zero when the plane actually contains B.

questions.q: She writes ε₁ = −N₁ dΦ_B/dt and ε₂ = −N₂ dΦ_B/dt, then divides to get ε₂/ε₁ = N₂/N₁. The ratio carries no minus sign because
options: a minus sign has been dropped, and it should be ε₂/ε₁ = −N₂/N₁.
the two minus signs and the shared dΦ_B/dt all cancel in the division.
the flux through the secondary is opposite in sense to that through the primary.
the emfs are magnitudes, so signs never appear in them.
questions.why: One flux threads both coils, so dΦ_B/dt is the same in both equations and divides out, and the two minus signs divide out with it. That is why the induced emf per turn is the same in the two coils and why equation 2 is sign-free — nothing was lost. The flux is shared, not reversed; and emf is a signed quantity, which is exactly why the cancellation is worth noticing.

questions.q: The step from ε₂/ε₁ = N₂/N₁ to V₂/V₁ = N₂/N₁ is justified by
options: the ideal-transformer assumption that each winding's induced emf equals its terminal voltage.
simple algebra, since emf and terminal voltage are the same quantity.
the conservation of energy, I₁V₁ = I₂V₂.
the fact that the two windings have the same resistance.
questions.why: Her slide 9 supplies the assumption explicitly: 'in an ideal transformer, the induced emfs ε₁ and ε₂ … are equal to the terminal voltages'. Only then does equation 3 follow, so it is a physical idealisation and not a manipulation. Emf and terminal voltage are different quantities in general — a real winding has resistance, and that is where the 90 % to 99 % efficiency goes; the power equation is a separate statement about currents; and equal winding resistances are neither assumed nor true.

questions.q: A 960 W coffeemaker designed for a 240 V line is to be run from a 120 V supply. The transformer needed has
options: N₂/N₁ = 1/2, a step-down transformer.
N₂/N₁ = 2, a step-down transformer.
N₂/N₁ = 4, a step-up transformer.
N₂/N₁ = 2, a step-up transformer.
questions.why: The primary is always the side connected to the input source, so V₁ = 120 V from the line and V₂ = 240 V at the appliance: N₂/N₁ = V₂/V₁ = 240/120 = 2, and since N₂ > N₁ this is by definition a step-up transformer. Getting the primary and secondary the wrong way round inverts every part of the problem; step-up and step-down are defined by the TURNS, N₂ > N₁ and N₂ < N₁; and the ratio is 2, not its square.

questions.q: The same coffeemaker draws, from the 120 V line,
options: 8.0 A, while 4.0 A flows in the coffeemaker itself.
4.0 A, while 8.0 A flows in the coffeemaker itself.
8.0 A on both sides, since the current is the same throughout.
4.0 A on both sides, since power is conserved.
questions.why: P_av = V₁I₁ gives the line current I₁ = 960/120 = 8.0 A, and the secondary carries I₂ = 960/240 = 4.0 A. Check with I₁V₁ = I₂V₂: 8.0 × 120 = 4.0 × 240 = 960 W. Stepping the voltage UP by two steps the current DOWN by two, so the appliance side carries the smaller current — swapping them is the standard error. The current is not the same on both sides, and conservation of power is precisely what makes them different.

questions.q: The coffeemaker's own resistance, from V₁/I₁ = 120/8 = 15 Ω, is
options: 30 Ω, because R = (V₁/I₁)(N₂/N₁) = 15 × 2.
15 Ω, the value already computed.
7.5 Ω, because R = (V₁/I₁)/(N₂/N₁).
60 Ω, because R = (V₁/I₁)(N₂/N₁)² = 15 × 4.
questions.why: Her formula is V₁/I₁ = R/(N₂/N₁)², with the turns ratio SQUARED, so R = 15 × 2² = 60 Ω — confirmed independently by V₂/I₂ = 240/4.0 = 60 Ω. Applying the ratio to the first power gives 30 Ω and is the single commonest error with this formula; 15 Ω is what the line APPEARS to be driving, not what the appliance is; and dividing instead of multiplying goes the wrong way for a step-up transformer.

questions.q: A 1600 W, 120 V hair dryer is run from a 240 V outlet through an ideal transformer. Its apparent resistance seen from the 240 V side, and its own actual resistance, are
options: 36 Ω and 9 Ω.
36 Ω and 144 Ω.
9 Ω and 36 Ω.
36 Ω and 18 Ω.
questions.why: I₁ = 1600/240 = 6.67 A, so V₁/I₁ = 36 Ω — which is where her slide stops, and it is the correct answer to the question 'what resistance will your dryer APPEAR to have'. The dryer's own resistance needs the missing line, R = (V₁/I₁)(N₂/N₁)² = 36 × (1/2)² = 9 Ω, confirmed by V₂/I₂ = 120/13.3 = 9 Ω. 144 Ω multiplies by the ratio squared the wrong way round; the pair 9 Ω and 36 Ω swaps apparent and actual; and 18 Ω uses the ratio to the first power.

questions.q: The core of a transformer is laminated, and a transformer produces no output on a steady DC supply. The reasons are
options: lamination reduces hysteresis loss; DC gives no changing flux, so no emf is induced.
lamination interrupts eddy currents in the core; DC gives no changing flux, so no emf is induced.
lamination increases the flux; DC is blocked by the insulation between the laminations.
lamination reduces copper loss in the windings; DC changes the frequency of the output.
questions.why: Her slides say the core is 'made up of thin sheets of metal that are insulated from each other' specifically 'to minimize eddy current losses', and the whole of equation 1 is a d/dt, which is why a transformer 'can only be used with AC'. Hysteresis is never mentioned in the deck and is not what lamination cures; lamination does not increase the flux, and the insulation blocks currents in the core rather than blocking DC in the windings; copper loss lives in the windings, not the core, and the frequency of a transformer's output always equals that of the source.
